title: Halfjaarbericht 2026 (half-year report, Havenbedrijf Rotterdam N.V.)
bib_title: Halfjaarbericht 2026: throughput, container capacity and the Strait of Hormuz effect
date_evidence: Bestuursverklaring en beoordelingsverklaring Deloitte Accountants B.V., gedateerd 17 juli 2026 (Halfjaarbericht 2026)
key_claim: Total throughput in the port of Rotterdam reached 212.0 million tonnes in H1 2026, up 0.4%; container volume fell 0.1% in TEU; transhipment fell 20% for lack of terminal capacity, with additional capacity at several container terminals from the end of 2026; oil product throughput rose 11.5% on Hormuz-linked refinery runs.
frame_summary: Argues that Rotterdam is resilient against war and trade disruption but capacity-bound in containers, with the constraint easing only when new terminal capacity arrives from the end of 2026.

title: October Sees Near Daily Strikes on Ships in Hormuz
bib_title: October sees near daily strikes on ships in Hormuz
key_claim: A ship has been struck in the Strait of Hormuz nearly every day in October; nine ships, mostly crude tankers, were hit between 1 and 6 October, the week to 7 October saw 12 attacks, the highest weekly total of the war, while Lloyd's List Intelligence counted 143 transits in the same week and September's 477 non-Iranian transits were the highest since the conflict began.
frame_summary: Argues that the strike-and-shuttle pattern now moving near pre-war oil volumes through a contested strait is not a sustainable new normal, against official claims that the strait is effectively open.

title: Container shipping faces 2027 pressure as huge orderbook hits the water
bib_title: Container shipping faces 2027 pressure as huge orderbook hits the water (BIMCO outlook)
key_claim: BIMCO expects container fleet capacity to grow 4.6% in 2026 and another 9% in 2027, with more than 14 million TEU on order, about 42% of the existing fleet; 2027 demand growth is forecast at 0.5% to 2.5% if Hormuz remains closed and 2.5% to 4.5% if normal traffic resumes, and gradual Suez normalisation could cut ship demand growth by about five percentage points.
frame_summary: Argues that the container market's fate in 2027 is set by an orderbook already contracted, with war-driven rerouting the only thing deferring the oversupply reckoning.
